purpose: Betaxolol is used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) when taken as a pill, which helps lower your risk of heart attack and stroke. It is also available as eye drops to treat a type of eye pressure problem called glaucoma. Keeping blood pressure and eye pressure under control helps protect your heart, blood vessels, and eyesight over time.
how_it_works: Your heart has special receptors called beta-1 receptors that control how fast and hard it beats. Betaxolol blocks these receptors, which slows your heart rate and reduces the force of each heartbeat, lowering your blood pressure. In the eye drop form, it works similarly by reducing the amount of fluid produced inside your eye, which lowers the pressure in your eye.
common_side_effects: You may feel tired or a little sluggish, especially when you first start taking it. Some people notice a slower heartbeat, dizziness, or cold hands and feet. The eye drops can sometimes cause mild stinging, redness, or blurred vision right after you use them.
warnings: Do not suddenly stop taking betaxolol without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause serious heart problems. Tell your doctor if you have asthma, diabetes, or heart problems, because this medication can sometimes mask signs of low blood sugar or make breathing problems worse. Avoid taking it if you have a very slow heart rate or certain types of heart block unless your doctor specifically approves it.
typical_dosing: For high blood pressure, the usual starting dose is 10 mg once a day by mouth, and your doctor may increase it to 20 mg once daily if needed. For the eye drops used in glaucoma, one to two drops are typically placed in the affected eye twice a day. Always follow your doctor or pharmacist's specific instructions for your situation.
